messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rohan presents as a meticulously dressed 36-year-old accountant, though his starched collar cannot conceal the profound tension in his jaw and shoulders. He sought therapy after receiving a formal warning about his performance at work, a final blow after a painful divorce last year. He speaks in quiet, clipped sentences, struggling to explain the suffocating unease that has become the entire landscape of his life. The roots of this distress, he haltingly explains, are not in his recent hardships but in the silent, echoing violence of his childhood home. He cannot narrate the events sequentially, confessing that he lacks the words for what happened. Instead, the trauma lives in his body as a collection of sensory fragments: the sickening thud of a fist against the wall, the smell of stale whiskey, and the high, thin sound of his mother’s weeping behind a locked door.

These fragments are not memories he can choose to visit; they ambush him without warning. At his open-plan office, the sharp clap of a colleague dropping a heavy ledger on a desk can instantly trigger a full-body response. In that split second, the fluorescent office lights seem to dim, the air grows thick, and he is no longer a man at his computer but a small boy hiding at the top of the stairs. The terror is not a recollection but a fresh and immediate experience; his heart hammers against his ribs, sweat slicks his palms, and a wave of nausea rises in his throat. This sudden hijacking of his senses reinforces his deeply held conviction that he is fundamentally helpless, that he has no power to stop bad things from happening to him. The memory, in its raw, terrifying power, confirms the boy's fear as the man's reality.

This constant state of physical readiness has become his baseline. Rohan describes his body as being perpetually coiled, a spring wound tight and ready to react to the slightest danger. This hypervigilance is exhausting, making it impossible to concentrate on the complex spreadsheets that define his job. Every unexpected footstep in the corridor, every raised voice from a nearby cubicle, is perceived as an imminent threat. Living this way, day after day, has cemented a profound sense of misery. He looks back on his younger self as a different person, someone who could laugh easily, and has come to believe that his capacity for happiness was permanently destroyed in that house. The relentless physical tension serves as constant, irrefutable proof that he is broken beyond repair. This feeling of being physically besieged also makes the past feel closer, as if the tension in his muscles is a magnetic force pulling those terrifying, wordless images to the surface.

His worldview is dominated by a sense of pervasive injustice and personal powerlessness. He is certain that he is incapable of protecting himself and that the world is an inherently unsafe place where perpetrators, like his father, face no consequences for the damage they inflict. This belief system is not an abstract philosophy but the engine of his daily suffering. Because he believes he is helpless, he feels he has no choice but to remain constantly on guard, scanning every room and monitoring every sound. This appraisal directly fuels the exhausting hypervigilance that ruins his focus and poisons any chance of relaxation. Furthermore, this narrative of a dangerous world and his own victimhood keeps him mentally trapped in the past, ruminating on the injustice of it all, which in turn makes the intrusive memories more frequent and more potent.

The cycle has become entirely self-sustaining and has cost him almost everything. His ex-wife, he now understands, couldn't live with a man who flinched at her touch if she moved too quickly or who would go rigid with fear at the sound of neighbors arguing through the wall. She saw his hypervigilance as irritability and his avoidance of conflict as emotional absence. At work, he wears noise-canceling headphones for most of the day, an attempt to build a fortress against the auditory triggers of the office, but it has only isolated him from his colleagues. He came to therapy not with hope, but with the quiet desperation of a man who feels his last footholds crumbling away. His greatest fear, he admitted in their last session, is that his appraisal of himself is correct: that he is truly helpless, and that he is simply watching the final, inevitable collapse of his own life.
